analysis.one_liner: Funds a broad package of maternal health programs and extends WIC nutrition aid for new mothers to two years.
analysis.headline: The Momnibus Act was introduced in the Senate with 29 original sponsors, all Democrats or independents, and was referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which has taken no further action on it.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill, often called the "Momnibus," is a package of maternal health programs. It extends WIC food and nutrition benefits for new mothers from six months to 24 months after pregnancy, sends grants to community organizations and health departments in areas with high maternal death rates and poverty, pays to train and grow the maternal care workforce (midwives, doulas, nurses), and funds data collection and studies aimed at ending preventable deaths from pregnancy and childbirth. It also addresses care for incarcerated pregnant people, veterans, and Native communities, and authorizes steady federal funding through 2031.
analysis.who_benefits: Pregnant and postpartum people, especially those in groups with the highest maternal death rates — Black, Native, rural, low-income, incarcerated, and veteran mothers. The bill would also create paid work for doulas, community health workers, midwives, and community organizations serving new mothers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Pregnant and postpartum mothers, especially underserved groups

how_it_helps.text: Doubles the WIC postpartum eligibility window from six months to 24 months, and extends the breastfeeding eligibility period to 24 months, so new mothers keep nutrition benefits for two years after pregnancy instead of six months.

Authorizes $100 million per year (fiscal 2027-2031) for grants to community organizations, tribes, and health departments to address housing, transportation, nutrition, and other non-medical causes of maternal deaths, with priority for high-poverty areas with high maternal mortality.

Authorizes another $100 million per year for community-based maternal health equity programs, plus funding for anti-bias and respectful care training in hospitals ($5 million/year) and grants to grow and diversify the midwife, doula, and maternal nursing workforce ($15 million per program per year).

Creates a federal task force across housing, transportation, agriculture, and health agencies to coordinate action on the causes of maternal deaths, and funds maternal mortality review committees, studies of maternal health among American Indian and Alaska Native people, and maternal mental health programs.
Bars the shackling of pregnant people in federal custody and funds model programs and grants to improve care for incarcerated pregnant and postpartum people.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through roughly $260 million per year in newly authorized spending through fiscal 2031, plus open-ended authorizations for several data and compliance programs. Hospitals, health systems, and insurers also take on new training, reporting, and bias-compliance requirements when they accept the bill's grants.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers; hospitals and insurers take on requirements

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes roughly $260 million per year in new federal spending through fiscal 2031, plus several sections funded by 'such sums as may be necessary' with no dollar cap.

Many of its fourteen titles are task forces, studies, reports, and pilot programs rather than direct delivery of care, so a large share of the money could go to administration and research before reaching patients.

Hospitals and health systems that take the grants must build bias-reporting compliance programs and publicly report patient-experience and bias-case data, a real compliance cost and reputational exposure for providers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefits — longer WIC eligibility, funding for community maternal health programs, and a larger midwife and doula workforce — target one of the starkest gaps in American health: the United States has by far the highest maternal death rate among wealthy nations, concentrated among Black and Native mothers. The costs are modest by federal standards, though the bill's heavy reliance on studies, task forces, and pilot projects means some of the money may not reach patients quickly. The hospital accountability provisions could be strengthened — the compliance programs are voluntary and grant-funded rather than mandatory.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Health committee, where it has sat without a hearing or vote since early August, with Congress adjourning in early January 2027.

narrative.text: Senator Cory Booker introduced the Momnibus Act on August 6, 2026, with 28 cosponsors joining him as original sponsors — 27 Senate Democrats and 1 independent — for 29 sponsors in all.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day it was introduced.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote appears in the bill's action history after the referral.
Congress remains in session until January 3, 2027, so the bill is technically alive, but it was introduced with roughly five months left in the two-year Congress and no Republican cosponsors.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has changed position — the bill simply sits in committee. The status quo persists: hospitals and insurers face no new maternal care accountability requirements, and no new money flows to maternal health programs, so nothing has improved for the mothers the bill targets.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The status quo; no new programs or rules yet

sides.party_line_note: All 29 sponsors are Democrats or independents; no Republican senator cosponsored the bill, and the Republican-run committee it sits in has not moved it.

industries.note: The bill offers hospitals grant money but, in exchange, requires bias-reporting compliance programs and public reporting of patient-experience and bias-case data in maternity care. Hospitals' interest in avoiding public accountability for discrimination in childbirth care runs against the patients the bill protects.

industries.industry: Health insurers and Medicaid managed-care plans
industries.note: The bill directs federal guidance to states to encourage insurers to cover and reimburse diverse maternity care teams, including midwives and doulas, and creates a perinatal care payment demonstration project. Insurers gain from structured payment models but could face pressure to pay for care teams they currently avoid covering.

industries.industry: Midwives, doulas, and community-based maternal health organizations
industries.note: The bill is a major funding source for these groups: grants for community maternal health programs, scholarships for midwifery and nursing students, and recognition of doulas and community health workers as part of the maternity care workforce. Their gain comes from expanding care to mothers who currently go without.

Title IX funds telehealth models in maternity care and grants for technology-enabled learning for pregnant and postpartum people, mainly benefiting mothers in rural and underserved areas with limited access to providers.

Extending WIC eligibility for new mothers from six months to 24 months keeps more participants in the program longer, routing more federal nutrition purchases through WIC-approved grocers and food producers. The added purchases feed mothers and infants who would otherwise lose benefits.

analysis.trajectory: The bill was introduced with about five months left in the Congress, sits in a committee controlled by the other party, and has no Republican cosponsors. Bills at this stage — referred to committee, no hearing or markup, late in the session — almost never reach the floor. Expect it to die in committee in January unless leadership intervenes; its realistic path forward is reintroduction in the next Congress.
